question: "Constitutional morality acts as both a restraint and an enabler in a democratic society". Critically examine this statement in the context of recent judicial interpretations in India. (150 words)
candidate_answer:
Constitutional morality means following the values of the Constitution like equality, liberty and justice. The term was used by Dr Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly.

It acts as a restraint because it stops the government and the majority from doing anything against the rights of people. Courts use it to check arbitrary power.

It is also an enabler because it helps the marginalised get their rights. In Navtej Johar case the Supreme Court decriminalised homosexuality. In Sabarimala case women were allowed to enter the temple.

However some people say that judges are deciding moral issues and this is judicial overreach. The concept is also not clearly defined.

Thus constitutional morality is important for democracy.

question: Discuss the relevance and challenges of holding simultaneous elections in India. Would it strengthen federalism or undermine it? (150 words)
candidate_answer:
Simultaneous elections means holding Lok Sabha and state assembly elections together. A high level committee under Ram Nath Kovind has given its report on this.

Relevance:
- It will save money spent on elections
- Model code of conduct will not come again and again so development work will not stop
- Police and government staff will not be diverted often

Challenges:
- It needs constitutional amendments
- Regional parties are against it
- What will happen if a government falls in between
- Large number of EVMs and manpower will be needed

Federalism: It may strengthen federalism as centre and states will work together. But it can also weaken federalism as national issues will dominate and regional parties may suffer.

So government should take all parties on board.

question: The role of tribunals in India has expanded but concerns about their independence and effectiveness persist. Critically evaluate the current tribunal system in light of recent judicial and legislative developments. (150 words)
candidate_answer:
Tribunals are quasi judicial bodies set up to reduce the burden of courts and give faster and specialised justice. They were added to the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment in 1978 through Article 323A and 323B. Examples are NGT, CAT and ITAT.

They have expanded because courts are overloaded and many cases need technical knowledge.

Concerns:
- Appointments are controlled by the executive so independence is affected
- Many posts are vacant
- Lack of infrastructure
- Pendency of cases is high

Way forward: Appointments should be done by an independent body and vacancies should be filled on time. Tribunals should have proper infrastructure.

question: In light of increasing defections and political instability, do you think the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution needs a relook? Suggest reforms for strengthening anti-defection law. (150 words)
candidate_answer:
Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd Amendment in 1985 to stop defections of MLAs and MPs. Members can be disqualified if they leave their party or vote against the whip.

Need for relook: Defections are still happening and governments are falling in many states. The Speaker takes the decision on disqualification and he belongs to a party so he can be biased. Merger with two third members is allowed and this is misused. Decisions are also delayed by Speakers.

Reforms:
- Disqualification should be decided by the President or Governor on advice of Election Commission
- Time limit for Speaker to decide
- Defectors should not be made ministers

So anti defection law needs reform to strengthen democracy.

question: "The success of good governance lies in citizen-centric administration." Examine the significance of the Sevottam model in this context. (150 words)
candidate_answer:
Good governance means governance which is transparent, responsive and accountable. Citizen centric administration means putting citizens at the centre of government services.

Sevottam model was introduced by the Second ARC to improve public service delivery. It has three parts: citizen charter, public grievance redressal and service delivery capability.

Significance:
- Makes services time bound
- Improves accountability of officers
- Reduces corruption
- Increases satisfaction of citizens

Thus Sevottam helps in making administration citizen centric.

question: How do Self-Help Groups (SHGs) contribute to participatory governance in India? (150 words)
candidate_answer:
SHGs are small groups of people, mostly women, who save money together and give loans to each other. They are linked with banks under the SHG Bank Linkage Programme of NABARD. DAY-NRLM also promotes SHGs.

They contribute to participatory governance:
- Women take part in Gram Sabha and panchayat meetings
- They help in implementing government schemes at local level
- Many SHG members become panchayat members which gives leadership to women
- They create awareness about health and education

Challenges: lack of training, low literacy, dominance of elites, and lack of market linkages.

Thus SHGs help in bringing people into governance.

question: "The rise of technocracy in Indian governance risks depoliticizing policymaking". Critically examine its role in democratic governance. (150 words)
candidate_answer:
Technocracy means rule by experts and technical persons. In India many technocrats are appointed in government like Nandan Nilekani for Aadhaar and experts in NITI Aayog.

It helps in efficient governance as experts have knowledge. Policies become scientific and evidence based. Examples are Aadhaar, UPI and GST network. It also reduces corruption and increases transparency.

It also helps in delivery of services to the last mile with the use of technology.

Therefore technocracy is very useful for India and should be promoted more in governance.

question: How does PARAKH address assessment disparities and promote holistic education? Discuss the challenges associated with its implementation. (150 words)
candidate_answer:
PARAKH stands for Performance Assessment, Review and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development. It is a national assessment centre set up under NEP 2020. It works under NCERT.

It addresses disparities by setting common standards for all boards so that students from different boards are assessed equally. It conducts large scale surveys like National Achievement Survey. It promotes holistic education by focusing on competency based learning rather than rote learning.

Challenges:
- Education is in concurrent list so states may not agree
- Teachers need training
- Lack of infrastructure in rural areas
- Different languages

So it needs cooperation between centre and states.

question: What is Minilateralism? Examine the role of minilateral groupings such as the Quad and the Squad in countering China's assertiveness in the Indo-Pacific region. (150 words)
candidate_answer:
Minilateralism means cooperation between a small number of countries on a specific issue, unlike multilateralism where many countries are involved.

China is becoming assertive in the Indo-Pacific region with its actions in South China Sea and its String of Pearls strategy. So countries are forming small groups to counter it.

Quad is a grouping of India, USA, Japan and Australia. It works for free and open Indo-Pacific, maritime security and supply chains. Malabar naval exercise is conducted by these countries. Quad also works on vaccines and technology.

China calls Quad an Asian NATO but India says it is not a military alliance.

Thus Quad helps in checking China.

question: India's foreign policy is increasingly navigating a "post-Western" global order. Critically examine this trend and its strategic consequences for India's multilateral engagement. (150 words)
candidate_answer:
Post-Western order means a world where power is not only with the West but is shifting to Asia and the Global South. China and India are rising and groups like BRICS and SCO are becoming important.

India follows multi alignment and strategic autonomy. It is a member of Quad and also BRICS and SCO. India is the voice of Global South as seen in G20 presidency in 2023 when African Union was made permanent member.

Consequences: India gets more bargaining power and can help shape global rules. India needs reform of UN and UNSC seat.

So India should continue to balance and strengthen its economy.

question: "The Speaker plays a vital role in upholding the integrity of parliamentary proceedings, but increasing politicization has raised questions about the impartiality of the office." Critically examine the role, powers and challenges faced by the Speaker in the Indian parliamentary system. (250 words)
candidate_answer:
Speaker is the head of Lok Sabha. He is elected by the members of Lok Sabha. He conducts the proceedings of the house and maintains discipline.

Powers:
- Presides over meetings of Lok Sabha
- Decides admissibility of questions and motions
- Decides whether a bill is a money bill
- Decides disqualification of members under anti defection law
- Casting vote in case of a tie

Challenges:
- Speaker belongs to a political party so there are doubts on impartiality
- Opposition complains that they are not given time to speak
- Deputy Speaker post is kept vacant
- Delay in deciding disqualification cases
- Misuse of money bill route

Way forward: Speaker should resign from party like in UK. There should be a fixed time limit for disqualification cases. Election of Deputy Speaker should be done on time.

Thus Speaker should be neutral for proper functioning of Parliament.

question: The insertion of "Socialist" and "Secular" into the Preamble through the 42nd Amendment sparked enduring debates on constitutional morality and ideological identity. Examine the historical context and contemporary relevance of these additions. (250 words)
candidate_answer:
The words Socialist and Secular were added in the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act 1976 during the Emergency under the Indira Gandhi government. The 42nd Amendment is also called the mini constitution.

Historical context: In the Constituent Assembly, the demand to add these words was rejected by Dr Ambedkar as he felt that the economic and social system should not be fixed by the Constitution and people should decide. But the ideas were already present in Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights like Articles 25 to 28.

Debate: Some people say these words were added during Emergency without proper debate as opposition leaders were in jail. Some say they should be removed from the Preamble.

Supreme Court has said in cases like SR Bommai that secularism is part of basic structure.

Thus both words are part of our constitutional identity.

question: Discuss the statutory basis, jurisdiction, and functions of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) in India. Critically analyze the challenges to its autonomy and effectiveness. (250 words)
candidate_answer:
CBI was set up in 1965 on the recommendation of Santhanam Committee. It works under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act 1946. It is under the Ministry of Personnel. It is not a constitutional body.

Functions:
- Investigate corruption cases against central government employees
- Investigate big economic crimes
- Investigate serious cases referred by state governments or courts
- Coordinate with Interpol

Jurisdiction: CBI has jurisdiction in Union territories and needs state consent for investigating in states.

Challenges:
- Supreme Court called it a caged parrot
- Political interference
- Shortage of staff
- Low conviction rate
- Need of state consent

Way forward: Give statutory status to CBI, appoint Director by a committee and give financial autonomy.

Thus CBI should be made independent.

question: Discuss the causes and consequences of fiscal imbalance between the Centre and the states in India. How has the introduction of GST impacted the financial autonomy of states? (250 words)
candidate_answer:
Fiscal imbalance means the gap between the revenue of states and their expenditure responsibilities. In India the Centre has more revenue sources while states have more responsibilities like health, education and police.

Causes:
- Constitution gave major taxes to the Centre
- Cess and surcharge are not shared with states
- Centrally sponsored schemes need state share
- Poor tax base of states

Consequences: States depend on Centre for grants and are forced to borrow. This leads to conflict between Centre and states and affects development.

GST: GST was introduced in 2017 by the 100th Amendment. It is one nation one tax. GST Council has representatives of both Centre and states. States lost their power to fix taxes independently. But GST has made tax system simple and increased collection.

Finance Commission also helps by giving share in taxes to states.

Thus Centre and states should work together to solve this.

question: "The shift from 'government' to 'governance' has created a complex network of actors, but not necessarily accountability." Critically evaluate this statement in the Indian context. (250 words)
candidate_answer:
Government means the formal institutions of the state while governance means the process of decision making with participation of many actors like civil society, private sector and citizens. In India after 1991 reforms, governance has increased with privatisation and role of NGOs.

Many actors are now involved like regulators, NGOs, private companies and self help groups. Public private partnership is used in infrastructure. E-governance has increased citizen participation.

But accountability is a problem because when many actors are involved, it is not clear who is responsible. Private companies are not covered under RTI. Corruption and lack of transparency still exist. Citizens are not aware of their rights.

Way forward: Strengthen RTI, social audit and Lokpal. Digital literacy should be increased.

Hence governance is good but accountability should be ensured.

question: Despite multiple judicial pronouncements, police reforms remain elusive in India. Examine the systemic obstacles and suggest a viable roadmap. (250 words)
candidate_answer:
Police reforms are needed in India because police still works on the colonial Police Act 1861. Supreme Court gave directions in Prakash Singh case in 2008 such as State Security Commission, fixed tenure for DGP, separation of investigation from law and order and Police Establishment Board. But states have not implemented them fully.

Obstacles:
- Police is a state subject so states are not interested
- Political interference in transfers and postings
- Lack of manpower and infrastructure
- Corruption and poor image of police
- Lack of training

Roadmap:
- Implement Prakash Singh guidelines
- Separate law and order from investigation
- Increase police strength
- Training and use of technology
- Police complaints authority for accountability

Thus police reforms are necessary for rule of law.

question: "Affirmative action has achieved representation but not transformation". Critically analyze this statement in light of reservation policies and socio-economic data. (250 words)
candidate_answer:
Affirmative action means positive steps taken by the state to help disadvantaged groups. In India it is done through reservation for SC, ST and OBC in education, jobs and politics. Article 15(4) and 16(4) allow it. EWS quota of 10 percent was added by the 103rd amendment.

Representation achieved: Many SC and ST students have entered universities and government jobs. Women have 33 percent seats in panchayats. Political representation is there through reserved seats in Lok Sabha and assemblies.

Reservation has given opportunities to people who were earlier kept out of education and public life. It has also created a middle class among these communities.

Thus reservation has been successful in giving representation and it should continue.

question: "Capacity building is essential for ensuring inclusive growth and effective social justice delivery." Examine the role of capacity-building initiatives in improving outcomes in education, health, and skill development in India. (250 words)
candidate_answer:
Capacity building means developing skills, knowledge and abilities of individuals and institutions. It is needed for inclusive growth because people can participate in the economy only when they have education, health and skills.

Education: Samagra Shiksha and teachers training are helping to improve quality of education. Digital education like DIKSHA is also there. This improves learning outcomes.

Health: ASHA workers are trained to provide basic health services. Ayushman Bharat and health and wellness centres have improved access. Training of doctors and nurses is also being done.

There are challenges like low quality of training, shortage of staff and digital divide.

Therefore capacity building is important for social justice and it should be strengthened.

question: The expansion of BRICS reflects changing power dynamics in global politics. Discuss the strategic, economic, and diplomatic implications for India. (250 words)
candidate_answer:
BRICS is a grouping of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. It was formed in 2001. The term was coined by Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs. In 2024 it expanded to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE and others.

Strategic: India can use BRICS to balance the West and to increase its influence in the Global South. It is also good for India to have dialogue with China and Russia. But China dominates the group and India China border tensions are a problem.

Economic: New Development Bank gives loans for infrastructure. Trade with member countries can increase. De-dollarisation is being discussed but India is not in favour of it as it may harm relations with the US.

Diplomatic: India can get support for UNSC reform though China does not support it. India can raise the issue of terrorism. Expansion may reduce consensus in the group.

Thus India should keep balance between BRICS and Quad and protect its national interest.

question: "The strategic embrace of Israel and continued commitment to Palestine is a paradox that defines India's West Asia policy." Critically analyze this dual diplomacy. (250 words)
candidate_answer:
India recognised Israel in 1950 but established full diplomatic relations only in 1992. India has supported the Palestine cause since independence and was among the first non-Arab countries to recognise PLO. India has always supported the two state solution.

Relations with Israel: There is defence cooperation with purchase of Barak missiles, drones and Spike missiles. There is cooperation in agriculture and water technology. Trade and intelligence sharing on terrorism has also increased. PM Modi visited Israel in 2017.

Relations with Palestine: India gives aid to Palestine and has voted for Palestine at UN. India opened a representative office in Ramallah.

India follows a de-hyphenation policy where relations with both are separate. India also needs oil and gas from Arab countries and has a large diaspora there so it cannot ignore the Palestine issue.

After the October 2023 attack India condemned terrorism but also called for humanitarian aid to Gaza.
